title: Essays on Time
description: Ten calm, reflective essays on time: the long summers of childhood, railway time zones, the sundial and the atomic clock, waiting rooms, the patience of trees, deadlines and creativity, aging slang, music, the Sabbath and the archive.

lessons.title: The Long Summers of Childhood
lessons.summary: Why the summers of childhood felt so long, and how an adult can make the weeks feel fuller.
lessons.text:
Most of us remember the summers of childhood as enormous. Three months seemed to stretch ahead like a country road in the heat, and school was only a distant rumor. As adults, we watch the same three months pass in what feels like a long weekend. The calendar has not changed. Something in us has.

Psychologists offer a simple explanation, and it begins in the crib. For a baby lying in a crib, nearly everything is new: a face, the sound of rain, light on the ceiling. The brain records new experiences in rich detail, and when we later look back, a period full of detailed memories feels long. A child's summer is crowded with first times, and each one is stored with care, so the season grows in memory.

Adults, by contrast, live mostly among repetitions. We take the same train and eat the same lunch. The mind refuses to record every copy, so it condenses weeks of routine into a single impression. A month of ordinary afternoons may be condensed into one gray sentence: "I was busy." When we look back, little seems to have happened, and we conclude that time has rushed past us.

My own summers were spent at my grandparents' house by a lake. I remember the waterfront in great detail: the wooden dock, the old shed at the edge of the waterfront where my cousin and I kept our treasures. Behind the house, a field of rye moved in the wind like a slow, golden sea. We ran through the rye until our legs were scratched and our shirts were sweaty and stuck to our backs.

My cousin insisted that she was a mermaid. She would swim out to the dock, sit with her feet in the water and announce that a mermaid could not possibly come home for dinner. When our grandfather called from the porch, we answered with a loud whoop, and he would whoop back, which meant that we had ten more minutes.

Then there was bedtime, the great enemy of summer. Bedtime arrived while the sky was still light, and we lay awake, sweaty under a single sheet, sure that the best part of the day was happening without us.

I have only one snapshot from those years: two children in plastic sandals on the dock, narrowing their eyes at the sun. The sandals are bright green. It is a small, faded snapshot, but when I look at it, the whole summer returns, long and slow and full of firsts.

Perhaps that is the gentle lesson. We cannot become children again, but we can give our weeks a few more first times. The years may not slow down, but they will be better remembered.

Questions:
Why does a period full of new experiences feel long when we look back?
The brain records new experiences in rich detail, and a period full of detailed memories feels long.
What does the adult mind do with weeks of routine?
It condenses them into a single impression, so little seems to have happened.
What did the children answer when their grandfather called them?
They answered with a loud whoop, and he would whoop back.
Why did the children dislike bedtime?
Bedtime arrived while the sky was still light, and they were sure the best part of the day was happening without them.
What does the writer's only snapshot show?
It shows two children in bright green sandals on the dock.

lessons.title: The Day of Two Noons
lessons.summary: How the railways replaced local sun time with standard time and, in the end, with time zones.
lessons.text:
For most of human history, noon was a local event. It came when the sun stood highest over your own roof, so noon in one town arrived a few minutes before noon in the next town to the west. Nobody traveled fast enough to notice.

The railway changed that. A train could carry a passenger from London to Bristol in a few hours, and Bristol, which lies to the west, kept its clocks about ten minutes behind London. This was a real problem. A schedule printed in one city's time was misleading in another. At a busy interchange, where several lines met and passengers changed trains, the companies' clocks might disagree, and the travelers on the platform had to decide which clock to heed.

In Britain, the railway companies solved the problem by agreeing to designate London time as railway time for the whole network. Not every town was pleased. In Bristol, the clock on the old Corn Exchange was given a second minute hand, so that it could show both times at once. It still has two minute hands, a quiet record of a city that wished to keep its own noon.

In North America the problem was larger. By 1880, the railroads of the United States were using dozens of different local times. A Canadian engineer named Sandford Fleming began to argue for a system of time zones circling the globe, and his pamphlets were soon circulating among scientists and engineers. Each pamphlet made the same patient case for shared hours.

On November 18, 1883, the railroads of the United States and Canada adopted standard time zones. People called it the day of two noons, because in many towns the clocks were turned back and noon arrived twice. Not everyone heeded the change. Some citizens found it irrational that a railroad company should decide what time it was, and letters defending the sun were circulating in the press. A landowner on the outskirts of a small town might keep his own clocks on sun time for years, while the station on the outskirts of the same town kept railroad time. The landowner was not irrational; he was loyal to the sky.

The following year, scientists and statesmen from 25 countries met in Washington to choose a single starting line for the world's longitude. Not every statesman agreed, but the conference voted to designate the line through Greenwich, near London, as zero. The details took decades to finalize. The United States did not finalize its time zones in law until 1918.

Today the system seems natural. Yet each time we change our watch in a new time zone, we repeat, in a small way, the decision of those travelers on the platform: which clock to trust, the sun's or the one we share.

Questions:
Why did local times become a problem when the railway arrived?
A schedule printed in one city's time was misleading in another, and travelers at an interchange did not know which clock to heed.
How did the British railway companies solve the problem?
They agreed to designate London time as railway time for the whole network.
What is special about the clock on the Corn Exchange in Bristol?
It has two minute hands, so it can show both times at once.
Why was November 18, 1883, called the day of two noons?
In many towns the clocks were turned back, so noon arrived twice.
What did the statesmen and scientists decide in Washington?
They voted to designate the line through Greenwich as zero.

lessons.title: From Shadow to Atom
lessons.summary: The sundial, the quartz watch and the atomic clock, and why modern life depends on exact time.
lessons.text:
In my aunt's garden there is a small porcelain sundial, white with blue numbers, set on a stone column among the roses. As a child I thought it was a decoration. Only later did I understand that it is a scientific instrument, and one of the oldest kinds of instrument our species has made.

A sundial is beautifully simple. A thin blade casts a shadow on a marked face, and as the sun moves across the sky, the shadow moves from number to number. On a cloudy day, however, the light is diffuse. It comes from the whole sky at once, and diffuse light casts no clear shadow.

There is a pleasant theory that our clocks owe their direction to the sundial. In the Northern Hemisphere, the shadow travels clockwise, and the first mechanical clocks copied that motion. South of the equator the pattern is inverted, and the shadow moves the other way. Had clocks been invented in Australia, the word "clockwise" might describe the inverted direction.

The watch on my wrist works on another principle. A small battery of about one and a half volts sends a current through a crystal of quartz, which vibrates 32,768 times each second. The crystal is smaller than a grain of rice, and to see its fine shape, a watchmaker places it under a microscope. Under the microscope, it looks like a tiny tuning fork.

Yet even a good quartz watch gains or loses a few seconds each month. For science, that residual error is far too large, so physicists turned to the atom. An atom of cesium absorbs and gives off energy at an extremely regular rate, and since 1967 the second itself has been defined by that rate. The newest clocks go further still. Using lasers, they count the rhythm of atoms that absorb and release photons, the particles of light. Their residual error would add up to less than a second over the age of the universe. Several eminent physicists have received the Nobel Prize for work that made such clocks possible, and an eminent scientist's work rarely touches so many lives.

Why should ordinary people care? Because the satellites that guide our phones carry atomic clocks, and an error of a millionth of a second would place us hundreds of meters from where we really are. Our connectivity depends on exact time as well: networks and banks need their computers to agree about the hour. Even encryption, which keeps our messages private, relies in part on that agreement, since much modern encryption checks when a digital key was issued.

When I visit my aunt now, I like to stand by the porcelain sundial with my phone in my hand. The two instruments ask the same question, and the older one still answers it every sunny afternoon.

Questions:
Why does the sundial show no hour on a cloudy day?
On a cloudy day the light is diffuse, and diffuse light casts no clear shadow.
What happens to the shadow of a sundial south of the equator?
The pattern is inverted, and the shadow moves the other way.
What does the battery in a quartz watch do?
A small battery of about one and a half volts makes a tiny quartz crystal vibrate 32,768 times each second.
What do the newest clocks count?
They count the rhythm of atoms that absorb and release photons.
Why does our connectivity depend on exact time?
Networks and banks need their computers to agree about the hour, and even encryption relies on that agreement.

lessons.title: In the Waiting Room
lessons.summary: A reflection on waiting rooms, from the clinic to the bank, and the quiet company they offer.
lessons.text:
A waiting room is a strange kind of place. It exists only so that we may leave it, and the time we spend there belongs to no one. We sit, we look at the door, and we wait for our name.

Each waiting room has its own customs. In a doctor's office, the chairs are arranged along the walls so that no one has to face anyone else. When someone sneezes, every head rises for a moment, and there is a small hesitation before people return to their magazines, as if each of us were silently deciding whether to move one chair away. A second sneeze produces a longer hesitation.

At the pharmacy, the waiting is more public. We stand in a line while the pharmacist works behind the counter, counting pills with great patience. Now and then the pharmacist calls a name, and a person steps forward with relief, as if released from a spell.

The waiting room of a hospital emergency department is different again. It can be intimidating, with its bright lights, its screens and its doors that open only from the other side. Once, while I waited there with my father, a paramedic came through with a patient. The paramedic spoke calmly to the patient, then calmly to the nurse, and I noticed that the whole room seemed to breathe more slowly. A calm voice can reassure people who are not even being spoken to. Later that night, a young doctor came to reassure us that my father's injury was minor, and the room that had seemed so intimidating became simply a room with chairs.

Banks have their own way of waiting. In the bank near my office, customers stand behind a rope until a teller is free. Last week the man in front of me was explaining to the teller, in a low voice, that he needed more time for the repayment of a loan. The teller listened, nodded and found a way to spread the repayment over another year. I tried not to listen, and failed, and was glad for him.

The most comfortable waiting room I know is at the car dealership where I take my car for repairs. The dealership offers soft chairs, free coffee and a television that no one watches. Yet even there, the time feels borrowed, because our real lives are waiting outside in the parking lot.

What waiting rooms teach us, perhaps, is that our time is not entirely our own. It is tied to the time of the pharmacist, the paramedic and the teller, and to the time of strangers who sit beside us with the same patience. Seen this way, a waiting room is not empty time at all. It is a short lesson in sharing.

Questions:
What happens in the doctor's office when someone sneezes?
Every head rises, and there is a small hesitation before people return to their magazines.
Why can a hospital waiting room be intimidating?
It has bright lights, screens and doors that open only from the other side.
How did the paramedic change the mood of the room?
The paramedic spoke calmly, and the whole room seemed to breathe more slowly.
What did the man at the bank need?
He needed more time for the repayment of a loan, and the teller spread the repayment over another year.
What does the dealership offer people who wait?
It offers soft chairs, free coffee and a television that no one watches.

lessons.title: The Patience of Trees
lessons.summary: An old oak on a farm and the long, slow time that trees live in and record.
lessons.text:
At the edge of an old homestead in the hills, there is an oak that was planted, according to the family, by the first settlers who built the house. The homestead has changed many times since then. The barn has been rebuilt twice, and the road has been paved. The oak has simply continued, adding a little height each summer and a little width each year.

Gardeners divide plants into those that live for one season and those that return year after year. Plants of the second group are called perennials; roses, for example, are perennial. A tree, however, is the most perennial of all. An oak may live for several centuries, and some pines in the western mountains have lived for more than four thousand years. Next to such patience, a human life looks like a busy afternoon.

Trees are also planted by animals. Squirrels and other rodents bury acorns in autumn to eat during the winter, and each rodent buries far more than it later finds. The forgotten acorns become the next forest. In the woods behind the homestead, a wildcat sometimes rests along a high branch, and a wildcat can sleep in a tree for most of the day, unseen by everyone below.

The best way to read a tree's history is to look at its rings. When a sawyer at the local mill cuts through a log, the sawyer can count the rings, one for each year, and see where wide rings show good, wet summers and narrow rings show years of drought. Some rings show darker marks. A torrent of water in a flood year may leave its sign, because a torrent can tear at the roots and slow the tree's growth. Scientists have even used tree rings to date an earthquake. In the Pacific Northwest, they studied trees that died when the land sank during a great quake, and the rings helped them fix the quake in the year 1700.

Trees are patient, but they can be harmed. In recent decades, a small beetle from abroad has killed millions of ash trees in North America. Scientists tried to eradicate the invader, but it spread faster than they could follow. It is extremely difficult to eradicate an insect once it has found a home, and the invader has now become part of the landscape.

What can we learn from trees? Perhaps that growth does not need to be dramatic to be real. The oak at the homestead has never done anything sudden. It has simply added a ring each year, in good times and bad, until it became the tallest thing on the hill. Most of the important work of our lives may be done the same way, one quiet ring at a time.

Questions:
What is a perennial plant?
A perennial plant returns year after year instead of living for one season.
How do rodents help to plant forests?
They bury acorns and forget many of them, and the forgotten acorns become the next forest.
What can a sawyer learn by counting the rings of a log?
The sawyer can see the age of the tree and which summers were wet or dry.
How did scientists date the great quake in the Pacific Northwest?
They studied the rings of trees that died when the land sank.
Why was it hard to eradicate the invader that killed the ash trees?
It spread faster than scientists could follow, and it is very difficult to eradicate an insect once it has found a home.

lessons.title: Deadlines and the Creative Mind
lessons.summary: Why many writers and artists need a deadline, and why they also need time without one.
lessons.text:
Every aspiring writer believes, at first, that the perfect conditions for work are complete freedom: no schedule, no boss and no date on the calendar. Most experienced writers know the opposite. Freedom without limits tends to produce very little, and a great deal of literature has been written because an editor was waiting.

The word "deadline" itself once described a line that could not be crossed. Today it describes a line in time, and its effect on the mind is remarkable. A deadline turns a vague wish into a task. The aspiring novelist who has spent three years choosing the perfect first sentence may, with a deadline two weeks away, write fifty pages.

Of course, a deadline also has its dangers. Students know the temptation to cram, leaving all the work until the last night and then trying to do a month's thinking in a few hours. To cram for an exam may work once or twice, but what we cram rarely stays with us. The same is true of creative work done in panic. A shortcut taken at midnight often becomes a problem by morning, and the writer who relies on a shortcut in every chapter finds that the whole book feels hurried.

The best ideas seldom arrive while we are staring at the page. Many artists describe the "aha" moment as something that happens in the shower, on a walk or while washing dishes, when the mind is relaxed. The aha moment is not a gift from nowhere, though. It usually comes after weeks of hard work, when the mind has gathered its materials and needs only a moment of quiet to arrange them.

For this reason, some writers repeat a simple mantra: work hard, then step away. Another popular mantra holds that a first draft only has to exist, not to be good. Once it exists, the writer can revamp it, and the revamped second or third version is often where the real book appears.

I wrote most of my own first book in a rented room with a laptop whose lithium battery lasted barely two hours. Every evening, when the warning light came on, I knew I had to save my work and stop. The dying lithium battery became my small daily deadline, and I am not sure the book would exist without it. My anxiety, augmented by strong coffee, kept me typing until the very last minute, and the coffee probably augmented my mistakes as well.

Perhaps the truth is that two kinds of time are complementary. There is open time, when we wander, read and let ideas grow without pressure. And there is narrow time, when a deadline gathers everything into a finished shape. The two are not enemies but complementary seasons of the same work.

Questions:
What does a deadline do to a vague wish?
A deadline turns a vague wish into a task.
Why is it a poor idea to cram?
What we cram rarely stays with us, and work done in panic often has problems.
Where do many artists say the aha moment happens?
It happens in the shower, on a walk or while washing dishes, when the mind is relaxed.
How did the writer's lithium battery help with the first book?
It lasted barely two hours, so it became a small daily deadline.
Which two kinds of time are complementary?
Open time for wandering and narrow time with a deadline are complementary.

lessons.title: How Words Grow Old
lessons.summary: Slang ages faster than any other part of a language, and some of it becomes ordinary English.
lessons.text:
Language changes so slowly that we rarely notice it, except in one place. Slang is the part of a language that ages fastest, and it is therefore one of the best clocks we have. Hear a word of slang from your grandparents' youth, and you can almost see the clothes they wore.

Most slang begins as a kind of secret. A group of young people, or soldiers, or sailors, invents a word that outsiders do not understand. When the word spreads to everyone, it loses its secret, and the young move on to something new. Few things sound older than the slang of twenty years ago.

Some words, however, survive this process and become ordinary English. The word "savvy" is a good example. It probably comes from the Spanish or Portuguese words for "you know," picked up by sailors in distant ports more than two centuries ago. For a long time it was sailors' slang. Today, a newspaper can describe a savvy investor or a savvy shopper without a smile. The word has climbed, slowly, from the harbor to the front page.

Adjectives are especially restless. The adjective "nice" once meant foolish, and only after centuries did it come to mean pleasant. The adjective "awesome" used to describe something that filled people with fear and wonder, like a storm at sea; now it may describe a sandwich. When an adjective becomes too popular, its meaning wears thin, like a coin passed through too many hands.

Technology produces new words at an extraordinary rate. The word "nuke," a short form of "nuclear," first meant a nuclear weapon. About forty years ago, people began to use it in a gentler sense: they would nuke their leftovers in the microwave. Many people still nuke a cup of cold coffee. In the same way, "webcam" was once a bright new word for a camera attached to a computer. Now that every phone and laptop contains a camera, the webcam as a separate object is disappearing, and the word may someday sound as old-fashioned as "wireless" does for the radio.

Even the shape of the week has its slang. In many offices, Wednesday is called "hump day," because it sits at the top of the working week like the hump of a camel. Once you are over the hump, the weekend is in sight. The expression is cheerful, and it reflects something real: the middle of the week feels like the top of a hill.

To study slang, then, is to study time itself. Every generation leaves behind a layer of words, like the rings of a tree. Most of them fade, a few become standard, and all of them remind us that our own language will one day sound old to someone else.

Questions:
Why is slang one of the best clocks we have?
Slang is the part of a language that ages fastest, so a single word can show when someone was young.
Where does the word savvy probably come from?
It probably comes from the Spanish or Portuguese words for "you know," picked up by sailors.
How did the adjective nice change?
It once meant foolish, and only after centuries did it come to mean pleasant.
What does it mean to nuke leftovers?
It means to heat them in the microwave.
Why is Wednesday called hump day?
It sits at the top of the working week like the hump of a camel.

lessons.title: Music, the Art of Time
lessons.summary: A viola player remembers a summer tour with her quartet and reflects on music as shaped time.
lessons.text:
Painting fills space, but music fills time. A painting hangs on the wall all at once, and we may look at it in any order we like. A piece of music, by contrast, exists only as it passes. We cannot hear the end before the beginning, and once a note is gone, it is gone. Every concert shows how time feels when someone shapes it with care.

I learned this as a student, when I played the viola in a string quartet. The viola is the quiet member of the violin family, a little larger than the violin, with a darker, warmer voice. Nobody becomes famous for playing the viola, but a quartet without one sounds hollow, like a house without a middle floor. My own viola was old and slightly scratched. I had bought it at a knockdown price from a music shop that was closing, and the owner, sorry to see it go at such a knockdown price, told me to play it often so that it would not feel abandoned.

One summer, the four of us decided to tour the coastline. We had little money, so we went by bus and slept in a hostel in each town. A hostel is not built for musicians. The rooms were small, the walls were thin, and we practiced in the kitchen of one hostel while other guests cooked their pasta around us. Some of them stayed to listen.

Our concerts were arranged by a booker who worked for several small halls along the coastline. She was a practical woman who answered every question with a schedule. When we complained that one hall had only thirty seats, the booker reminded us that thirty people listening carefully are worth more than three hundred who are not. She was right, as she usually was.

The weather that summer was clement, warm and dry for weeks, and in two towns we played outdoors by the sea. Clement weather is a gift to musicians, because damp air makes strings go out of tune. I still remember one evening when the sun went down during a slow movement, and the light faded at almost exactly the pace of the music. For a few minutes, the time of the music and the time of the day seemed to be the same thing.

That is what music does best. A good performance can make five minutes feel like an hour or an hour feel like five minutes. A pause in the right place can make an audience hold its breath.

We are no longer students, and we live in different cities now. But every summer the quartet reunites for one week. When we reunite, we always begin with the piece we played on that first evening by the sea, and for the length of it, the years between seem to disappear.

Questions:
How is music different from painting?
A painting exists all at once, but music exists only as it passes.
How did the writer buy her viola?
She bought it at a knockdown price from a music shop that was closing.
Where did the quartet practice during the tour?
They practiced in the kitchen of a hostel while other guests cooked.
What did the booker say about the hall with thirty seats?
She said that thirty people listening carefully are worth more than three hundred who are not.
Why is clement weather a gift to musicians?
Damp air makes strings go out of tune, so warm, dry weather helps.

lessons.title: A Palace in Time
lessons.summary: The Jewish Sabbath and the old human idea that rest gives shape and meaning to time.
lessons.text:
Most of the great buildings of the world are made of stone. The Sabbath is a building made of time. Every week, from sunset on Friday until the stars come out on Saturday night, Jewish families who keep the Sabbath step out of the ordinary week and into a day that is set apart. One famous rabbi described it as a palace in time: a structure that cannot be touched, but that people enter together.

The day begins at home, before anyone goes to the synagogue. As the sun sets on Friday, candles are lit, and the candles symbolize the line between ordinary time and holy time. Two loaves of bread on the table symbolize the double portion of food that, according to the Bible, fell from heaven before the day of rest. Then many families walk to the synagogue, where a cleric leads songs that welcome the Sabbath like a bride.

The Sabbath also has a rich culinary tradition. Because cooking is set aside on the day of rest, it must be finished in advance. In many homes a slow stew is placed on a low heat before sunset and eaten warm the next day. This culinary custom is so old that, for many people, the smell of the stew is the smell of the Sabbath itself.

What people do not do on the Sabbath is just as important. Those who keep it shun work, business and, in many families today, phones and screens. To shun these things is not a punishment. It is a way of saying that a person is more than what he or she produces. Amidst a week of tasks, messages and noise, the Sabbath offers a day in which nothing needs to be achieved.

Many people who are not religious have borrowed the idea. Some vacate their offices at a fixed hour every Friday and leave email until Monday. Others vacate the city for a day without plans. They describe the experience as a kind of cleansing, a cleansing not of the body but of the attention, which has been pulled in a hundred directions all week.

A cleric I once spoke to told me that the Sabbath is not a break from life but its fulfillment. The week, he said, leads up to rest the way a road leads to a house. The fulfillment of six days of labor is the seventh. There is even an old saying that if everyone kept the Sabbath properly, the messiah would come. Whatever one believes about the messiah, the saying expresses a beautiful hope: that peace might begin with a single day well kept.

Perhaps that is the deepest lesson of the Sabbath. Time is not only something to be spent. It can also be something to be honored, shared and, once a week, simply lived in.

Questions:
What do the candles symbolize on Friday evening?
They symbolize the line between ordinary time and holy time.
What does the Sabbath offer amidst a week of tasks and noise?
Amidst a week of tasks and noise, it offers a day in which nothing needs to be achieved.
What do people who keep the Sabbath shun?
They shun work, business and, in many families, phones and screens.
Why do some people vacate their offices at a fixed hour on Friday?
They want a kind of cleansing of the attention, which has been pulled in many directions all week.

lessons.title: Letters in the Archive
lessons.summary: An archive of parish records, town lists and old letters, and the conversation it allows with the past.
lessons.text:
My interest in archives began in a used bookstore. On a high shelf, I found a bundle of letters tied with string. The owner of the bookstore had bought them with a box of old books and did not know whose they were. I paid a few dollars and carried them home, and that evening I began a conversation with people who had been dead for a hundred years.

That is what an archive is: not a store of dusty paper, but a conversation with the past.

To learn who had written the letters, I went to the regional archive. Its oldest records came from the diocese, which for centuries had kept the registers of every baptism, marriage and burial in its parishes. In the records of the diocese I found the letter writer's family, generation after generation, written in brown ink by priests long ago.

The archive also kept the old town rolls. In earlier centuries, a burgess was a citizen with the right to trade and to vote in town affairs, and each new burgess was written into the list. The letter writer's great-great-grandfather had been a burgess, a baker who paid his fee in 1790 and signed his name with care. Beside the list was another treasure: a letter from a sailor of that town who had been abducted by pirates in the Mediterranean. He wrote from captivity, asking his family to raise money for his release. A note on the back said that the money had been paid. The sailor abducted by pirates came home.

The letters from the bookstore were written by a young man who decided to enlist in the army in 1917. Many young men chose to enlist that year, and most of his letters went to his fiancée, a teacher in the same town. He wrote about mud, bad food and the songs the soldiers sang, and he asked his fiancée to describe the garden, the weather and the market.

Soldiers' letters were read by officers before they were sent, so the couple invented a covert code. A small cross under a word meant "I miss you," and a circle meant "Do not worry." The code was covert, but the little crosses appear on almost every page.

Early in 1919, the letters stop abruptly. For a long and anxious moment, I feared the worst. Then, in the archive, I found the record of a marriage in the summer of 1919: the soldier and his fiancée, married in the town church. The letters had stopped abruptly for the happiest of reasons. He had come home, and there was no longer any need to write.

An archive cannot give us the whole past. But it lets us hear voices that would otherwise be silent, and it reminds us that we, too, are writing letters to readers we will never meet.

Questions:
Where did the writer find the bundle of letters?
The writer found them on a high shelf in a used bookstore.
What records did the diocese keep?
The diocese kept the registers of every baptism, marriage and burial in its parishes.
What was a burgess?
A burgess was a citizen with the right to trade and to vote in town affairs.
What happened to the sailor who was abducted by pirates?
He wrote from captivity, his family paid the money, and he came home.
Why did the letters stop abruptly in 1919?
The soldier had come home and married his fiancée, so there was no need to write.
